plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two panels, (a) and (b), tracking ten fractional values through a bucket sort. Panel (a) is a vertical column of ten gray cells headed by the italic letter A, with row indices 1 through 10 running down its left side; from top to bottom the cells hold .78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, and .68. Panel (b) is a second vertical column of ten gray cells headed B and indexed 0 through 9, each cell serving as the head of a linked list. The cells at indices 0, 4, 5, and 8 contain only a diagonal slash. The rest carry a horizontal arrow into a chain of two-field records, each record showing a value on the left and either a pointer arrow or a terminating slash on the right: index 1 leads to .12 then .17, index 2 to .21, .23, then .26, index 3 to .39 alone, index 6 to .68, index 7 to .72 then .78, and index 9 to .94. Each chain is in increasing order, and the leading digit of every value matches the index of the cell whose chain holds it, which is the correspondence the two columns invite the reader to check. The panels walk through distributing numbers drawn from the half-open interval from 0 to 1 into equal-width buckets, after which concatenating the sorted lists in index order gives the sorted output.

interactionPlan.concept: Bucket sort distributes n numbers uniformly drawn from [0,1) into n equal-width buckets using the index floor(n·x), keeps each bucket's list sorted by insertion, and then concatenates the buckets in index order to produce the sorted output.

demo_steps.title: The unsorted input
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a) holds ten numbers drawn from [0,1) in arbitrary order. Panel (b) starts as ten empty buckets, each the head of a linked list.

demo_steps.title: One element, one bucket
demo_steps.narration: Press step: A[1] = .78 is read, floor(10 × .78) = 7 highlights bucket 7 and its interval [0.7, 0.8), and a new node is drawn on that chain.

demo_steps.title: Insertion keeps each chain sorted
demo_steps.narration: When .12 arrives after .17, it is spliced ahead of it rather than appended, so bucket 1 reads .12 → .17. Each chain stays sorted as it grows.

demo_steps.title: The half-open convention
demo_steps.narration: Drag the probe across a bucket boundary: at x = 0.9 the value jumps into bucket 9 and stays there all the way to 0.999, so .94 can never spill into a tenth bucket.

demo_steps.title: Concatenate in index order
demo_steps.narration: All ten values are distributed; reading buckets 0 through 9 head-to-tail gives .12 .17 .21 .23 .26 .39 .68 .72 .78 .94 — the sorted output, with no comparison between buckets ever needed.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The bucket index floor(10x) already encodes the coarse ordering, so sorting reduces to tidying up tiny lists — concatenating the buckets in index order needs no comparisons across buckets at all.

Left panel: header italic 'A', a single vertical stack of ten light-gray bordered cells with black serif indices 1–10 to their left and values .78 .17 .39 .26 .72 .94 .21 .12 .23 .68 top to bottom; caption '(a)' below. Right panel: header italic 'B', a matching vertical stack of ten light-gray cells indexed 0–9; cells 0, 4, 5, 8 contain a thin diagonal slash (NIL). Nonempty cells emit a horizontal black arrow to the right into a chain of two-field gray records — left field value, right field either a short pointer stub feeding the next arrow or a diagonal NIL slash. Chains, aligned on the row of their bucket and extending rightward: 1 → .12, .17; 2 → .21, .23, .26; 3 → .39; 6 → .68; 7 → .72, .78; 9 → .94. Caption '(b)' below. Bucket 2's chain is the longest and defines the figure's right edge. Add a faint horizontal 0-to-1 number line beneath panel (b) divided into ten equal ticks for the boundary probe, with the active interval shaded. Use one accent color (e.g. amber) for the currently read A cell and a second (e.g. blue) for the targeted bucket and newly inserted node; keep everything else grayscale so the touched elements read instantly during replay.

authoredContext:
Bucket sort assumes that the input is drawn from a uniform distribution and has an average-case running time of O.n/. Like counting sort, bucket sort is fast because it assumes something about the input. Whereas counting sort assumes that the input consists of integers in a small range, bucket sort assumes that the input is generated by a random process that distributes elements uniformly and independently over the interval Œ0; 1/. (See Section C.2 for a definition of uniform distribution.) Bucket sort divides the interval Œ0; 1/ into n equal-sized subintervals, or buckets, and then distributes the n input numbers into the buckets. Since the inputs are uniformly and independently distributed over Œ0; 1/, we do not expect many numbers to fall into each bucket. To produce the output, we simply sort the numbers in each bucket and then go through the buckets in order, listing the elements in each. Figure 8.4 shows the operation of bucket sort on an input array of 10 numbers.
To see that this algorithm works, consider two elements AŒi and AŒj . Assume
without loss of generality that AŒi _x0014_ AŒj . Since bnAŒic _x0014_ bnAŒj c, either
element AŒi goes into the same bucket as AŒj  or it goes into a bucket with a lower
index. If AŒi and AŒj  go into the same bucket, then the for loop of lines 7–8 puts
them into the proper order. If AŒi and AŒj  go into different buckets, then line 9
puts them into the proper order. Therefore, bucket sort works correctly.
To analyze the running time, observe that all lines except line 8 take O.n/ time
in the worst case. We need to analyze the total time taken by the n calls to insertion
sort in line 8

discrepancies: The generated default view adds a number line (0–1 with ten tick intervals, a blue probe arrow and the annotation 'x = .94 → ⌊10x⌋ = 9') below panel (b) that does not exist in the source figure; its text renders at ~5–7 px at inline size and is effectively illegible.

In the default (step-0) state bucket 9 is wrapped in a blue dashed highlight box and a blue interval band is painted on the number line, adding colour to a purely black-and-grey source figure, so it is not a perfectly neutral drop-in replacement.

The linked-list node boxes are somewhat narrower/shorter relative to the B column than in the source (source nodes are roughly the same height as a bucket cell), making the chains look slightly cramped versus the original proportions.

The 'x = ...' probe caption sits directly above the number line and near the tick digits; combined with the tiny tick labels ('0 0 1 2 ... 9 1') the lower strip reads as visual clutter rather than a clean annotation.
evaluation.notes: The core CLRS bucket-sort figure (array A 1–10, buckets B 0–9, correctly ordered chains, NIL slashes, two-field nodes with next-pointer arrows) is reproduced accurately and the interaction set (demo steps, distribution stepper, probe slider, concat toggle, sandboxed code workbench with frame playback) is rich and conceptually apt; the main weaknesses are the extra number-line strip with illegibly small labels and blue highlighting that intrudes on the otherwise faithful default state.
action_items: Increase the number-line tick and probe-annotation font sizes (roughly double them relative to the 1060-unit viewbox) or move that strip into an optional overlay so it is readable at inline size.

Make the step-0 state fully neutral: suppress the blue dashed bucket-9 highlight, the probe band and the number line until the user moves a control, so the default render matches the greyscale source exactly.
Enlarge the linked-list node boxes (match node height to bucket-cell height as in the source) and keep the key/pointer divider proportions closer to the original.
Guard against the probe caption colliding with the tick digits by shifting it above the arrow with clearance, or draw it with a background plate.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; the issues are concrete rendering fixes (font sizes, default-state neutrality, node box proportions, label collisions) that belong to the generator.
